messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

On a bright spring afternoon, 19‑year‑old Anika, a hairdresser in a bustling downtown salon, was hurrying home after a long shift when a delivery truck lost its lane and veered into the crosswalk. She was the only one on the sidewalk, and the truck’s brakes failed to stop in time. The collision sent a concrete slab tumbling onto the road, shattering glass, and in a split second the world became a blur of headlights and screeching metal. The accident left a woman seriously injured, and Anika felt the crushing weight of guilt that she had somehow caused it. Even months later, the memory of that instant lingers as a vivid, sharp image in her mind, each replay punctuated by the thud of tires and the shriek of broken glass. The memory is accompanied by intrusive thoughts of the scene, a sudden rush of loud noises—her own racing heart and the blaring horns—and a mental replay of cars colliding with such ferocity. These triggers—intrusive thoughts, crash imagery, and loud noises—reawaken the day after the event, when she hears traffic or hears a sudden clatter. In those moments Anika finds herself unable to relax even when she knows she is in a safe environment, and she scans every room for exits, feeling as though danger could burst from any corner. The very triggers that summon the memory also awaken a sense of threat, causing her body to react strongly whenever she encounters something that reminds her of the accident. The vividness of the images, coupled with her inability to calm herself, fuels a belief that she cannot rely on others or on her own body; she feels the body has betrayed her by allowing her to be in a situation that could have been avoided. She also harbors the painful conviction that she failed to protect the injured woman, a thought that deepens her sense of failure. These negative appraisals feed back into her experience of the event, reinforcing the memory of the collision as a powerful, shame‑laden episode that she cannot escape. The triggers, the threat, and the negative appraisals together push her toward maladaptive strategies. She avoids the date of the accident, refusing to celebrate any anniversary that might remind her of the day. She also begins to fawn over clients and colleagues, becoming overly compliant and eager to placate anyone who might appear threatening. The fear of another crash or of being caught again in a dangerous situation leads her to avoid driving altogether; she refuses to drive, and she even resists being a passenger in a vehicle. These behaviors, while intended to keep her safe, become part of her daily routine, coloring her interactions at work and at home. As the months went on, the negative appraisals that had begun after the crash became entrenched. The belief that she could not rely on others and that her own body was unreliable made her retreat further into herself, reinforcing her feeling that the world was hostile. When she thought of the injured woman, the image of her lying on the asphalt, the thought that she had failed to protect her, she would see flashes of the crash, bringing back the same intrusive thoughts and loud noises. The memory, in turn, kept those negative appraisals vivid, as if the trauma were still unfolding. The sense of threat—unable to relax, constantly scanning for exits, and experiencing strong physical reactions—was now the backdrop to each day. The threat spurred her to continue avoiding driving and to become more compliant, as if compliance could neutralize a potential threat. Yet, each time she avoided driving or complied with others, the memory seemed to surface anew, reinforced by the fact that she was staying away from what she thought might be dangerous. The threat also made the triggers more potent, because the knowledge that she could be hurt again made the loud noises and crash imagery more jarring. All of these interactions kept the negative appraisals, triggers, and threat alive in a self‑reinforcing loop that seeped into every aspect of her life. Her maladaptive strategies—avoiding anniversaries, fawning over others, and shunning driving—became the visible face of her internal conflict. Each avoidance action triggered new memories of the crash, as she could not help but remember the sound of brakes squealing or the sight of a broken street. The strategies also fed back into her negative appraisals: every time she avoided a familiar day or became overly compliant, she felt more isolated, more unable to rely on others, and more certain that her body had failed her. The strategies themselves increased her sense of threat; the constant vigilance required to avoid driving kept her body in a state of hyper‑alertness, and the avoidance of anniversaries made her feel that the world could never be normal again. Finally, these strategies perpetuated the triggers: each time she avoided driving, she imagined the scene of the collision replaying in her mind, each image stoking the same intrusive thoughts and crash imagery she already feared. Now, at nineteen, Anika sits in the quiet of her apartment after closing the salon, her fingers hovering over the phone that she has been reluctant to answer for weeks. The thought of stepping outside, of hearing traffic, of hearing a sudden clatter, overwhelms her. Yet the fear of staying isolated, of feeling numb and helpless, is even greater. She has finally decided to seek help, because she can no longer tolerate the relentless cycle of thoughts that haunt her. She fears that if she does not change her patterns, her job and her relationship will unravel; she hopes that a therapist can help her find a way to trust herself and others again, to move beyond the images that no longer belong to her life.
